sections.title: Quick Answer
sections.content: **FaithWall** isn't a note-taking app — nothing beats a plain notes app for capturing what the pastor just said. What it does is keep one line alive after the service ends: log your notes in Apple Notes or GoodNotes, tag each entry with a date and reference, then let FaithWall turn the week's best takeaway into a lock-screen verse you actually see again.

sections.text: Search **sermon notes iphone app** and you'll find twenty roundups of note-taking apps, and all of them miss the real problem. Typing fast enough during a 35-minute sermon is a solved problem on any iPhone — Apple Notes, GoodNotes, Notion, all of them work fine. What's unsolved is everything that happens after you tap save. A note buried three weeks deep in an app you never reopen isn't a note anymore, it's digital landfill. FaithWall doesn't fix the note-taking half — your notes app already does that. It fixes the half where the note gets used again.
The sermon notes app that actually works: Notes, GoodNotes, or Notion?

Three apps cover almost everyone. **Apple Notes** is the default for a reason — it's already open, it syncs free across every device signed into iCloud, and you can dictate instead of type when your hands are full of a bulletin. **GoodNotes** costs money (a one-time purchase, no subscription as of this writing) but gives you a genuine notebook feel — handwriting with an Apple Pencil, PDF import if your church posts an outline in advance, and folders that keep months of notes from turning into one long scroll. **Notion** is overkill for most people and exactly right for a handful: if your calendar and reading plan already live there, a sermon-notes database that links to both is worth the setup. For everyone else, it's one more app to check. For where this fits into a fuller reading habit, see the [bible study tools pillar guide](/bible-study-tools-ios); for app-by-app picks beyond just notes, the [best free Bible apps for iPhone](/blog/best-free-bible-app-iphone) roundup covers ten of them in depth.

items: **Speed over features.** If capturing a thought takes more than two taps, you'll miss the next sentence.
**Search that actually works.** You'll search "the thing about anxiety from a few months ago" more often than you search a chapter reference.
**Export that isn't locked in.** Sermon notes outlive whatever app is trendy this year — pick one that lets you get your text back out.

sections.text: Where sermon notes actually die — and the 60-second fix

Here's what actually happens. You take good notes on Sunday. You mean to reread them Tuesday. Tuesday doesn't happen — dinner, a deadline, a kid who won't sleep — and by the time you remember, the note has scrolled off the first screen of the app and out of your head with it. The problem was never capture. It's retrieval. The fix is something that doesn't compete with your notes app — it just puts one line from it back in front of you, on your lock screen, every time you check your phone, which is most of the times you'd never open a notes app on purpose.

items: **Download FaithWall.** Free, no account required, set up in under a minute.
**Reread Sunday's notes once, Monday or Tuesday.** Pick the single line that actually changed something.
**Type that line in** as your verse or takeaway for the week.
**Let it rotate on your lock screen.** You'll see it more in one day than you'd have seen the original note in a month.

sections.text: A tagging system that survives past week three

Most **sermon notes iphone app** setups die at the same point — after capture, not during it. A system that survives adds three more fields to what you're already writing, and costs about ten extra seconds per entry. The same discipline sits behind [verse mapping on iPhone](/blog/verse-mapping-iphone-app): turning one passage into something you actually studied, not just heard.

items: **Date and reference.** Even a rough "Ephesians 2, mid-September" beats nothing — you'll want to find it again.
**One line of application.** Not what the pastor said — what you're actually going to do about it. This is the line that eventually goes on your lock screen.

**A single tag.** Pick from a short, fixed list — Identity, Suffering, Prayer, Community, whatever your church tends to preach on — so a search actually narrows things down instead of returning forty results.

sections.content: **Write the application line while the sermon is still going**, not after. The "what am I going to do about this" thought is sharpest in the room and gone within the hour — everything else in your notes can wait until the car. This pairs well with the tap sequence in [how to highlight verses on iPhone](/blog/how-to-highlight-verses-on-iphone) if you're marking your Bible itself, not just a notes app.

sections.text: For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks intently at his natural face in a mirror. For he looks at himself and goes away and at once forgets what he was like.

James isn't describing a bad note-taking system — he's describing what happens without one. The mirror shows something true and specific, and thirty seconds later the details are gone. A sermon works the same way if nothing carries the reflection past the parking lot.
The weekly review that keeps notes from becoming clutter

A five-minute Sunday-night or Monday-morning habit is the whole system: open the week's entry, reread it once, and decide whether the application line actually happened. If it did, archive it. If it didn't, that's the line worth keeping in front of you this week.

sections.label: of a congregation forgets the sermon by Wednesday
sections.description: Per a survey of church leaders reported by XPastor — the weekly review above is aimed directly at that gap, not at collecting more notes.

sections.content: **A note you never reread and a sermon you never heard end up in the same place.** The point of writing anything down was retrieval. If the system doesn't build in a reread, the notes app is just a nicer-looking way of forgetting.

sections.text: The literal answer to **sermon notes iphone app** is simple: Apple Notes or GoodNotes, whichever you'll actually keep opening. The complete answer is smaller than it sounds — a ten-second tag, a five-minute weekly reread, and one line each week promoted somewhere you can't avoid seeing it. Everything else is optional.
What's the best sermon notes app for iPhone?

Apple Notes covers almost everyone — free, already installed, syncs across devices. GoodNotes is worth the one-time cost if you want a handwriting feel or need to annotate a printed outline. Notion only makes sense if your calendar and reading plan already live there.
How do I actually remember my sermon notes later?

Capturing them is the easy part. Reread the week's entry once, on Monday or Tuesday, and pull out one line — the one that should actually change something. Put that line somewhere you'll see it without opening an app again, which is the gap worth closing.
Should I take sermon notes by hand or on my phone?

Whichever one you'll actually keep doing. Handwriting favors retention slightly, but a note you stop taking by week four loses to a system you never abandon. If typing on your phone means you're still doing it in six months, that's the better system for you specifically.
